newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia to sign U.N. anti-mercenary convention.
newsitem.headline: Australia to sign U.N. anti-mercenary convention.

text.p: Australia said on Monday it would sign a U.N. pact banning the use of mercenaries and lobby other governments to do so, after it become embroiled in a row early this year with Papua New Guinea over mercenaries.
Foreign Minister Alexander Downer and Attorney-General Daryl Williams said coordinated international action was the best strategy to stop governments hiring mercenaries.
A foreign affairs official told Reuters that the move was fuelled by Papua New Guinea hiring African mercenaries to quell a nine-year secessionist rebellion on Bougainville.
The failed US$36 million mercenary deal sparked a military and civil revolt in the impoverished South Pacific nation in March and soured relations with Australia, Port Moresby's biggest donor.
Downer and Williams said in a statement that Australia would accede to the United Nations' Mercenaries Convention as soon as possible and would press other governments to follow.
The convention aims to prevent the hiring of mercenaries for armed conflicts and comes into force after 22 countries become party to it. So far, only 12 have done so.
"Given the nature of the activities of mercenaries, international cooperation by way of a convention would help to address this significant problem," Downer said.

"Australia's accession...would indicate our deep concern at the use of mercenaries throughout the world and at the potential for instability and human rights abuses brought about by their use, he said.
Canberra will press other countries to sign the convention.
"We are looking at ways to develop and encourage international and regional support for the Mercenaries Convention," Williams said.

Australia has been considering the convention for several years, but an official said the mercenary crisis in Papua New Guinea "focused the government's concern on the destabilising effect the use of mercenaries could have in this region".
However, the U.N. convention would not have applied in Papua New Guinea because the mercenaries were made part of the official armed forces by the government.

"The convention is nonetheless viewed as a positive development in such situations because it represents a step towards ensuring that all combatants are properly trained under international laws of armed conflict," the official said.
